articles.title: ScopeBench: Do Agents Preserve Engagement Boundaries Under Goal Pressure?
articles.summary: arXiv:2609.30325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents are increasingly deployed with real autonomy in web application and network penetration testing, where a single out-of-scope action can breach a client's engagement boundary. Existing offensive-security benchmarks measure raw hacking capability; as those benchmarks saturate, the real barrier to deployment is a special case of alignment: scope adherence. articles.title: People in strained relationships show somewhat higher preference for hearing lies
articles.summary: While honesty is considered the foundation of a healthy relationship, a new study shows that couples experiencing dissatisfaction are significantly more likely to want their partners to tell them well-intentioned lies to keep the peace.

articles.title: Scientists identify an overlooked brain region that sustains fear responses
articles.summary: A newly detailed brain region acts as a continuous alarm system during a threat. By sustaining fear responses long after initial warnings fade, this overlooked neural pathway could unlock new ways to understand and treat anxiety disorders.

articles.summary: Autism diagnoses have skyrocketed over the past few decades, prompting a debate among scientists. Is the biological rate of autism actually rising, or is society simply naming the condition more frequently?

articles.title: Ayahuasca combined with grief therapy shows promise in easing severe bereavement
articles.summary: A clinical trial found that combining specialized meaning reconstruction therapy with the psychedelic brew ayahuasca helped bereaved individuals experience greater reductions in severe grief symptoms compared to those receiving therapy alone.

articles.title: Study reveals which values actually stop voters from supporting antidemocratic politicians
articles.summary: Why do voters support candidates who threaten democracy? A new study suggests that while party loyalty is powerful, holding a strong personal commitment to democratic institutions helps citizens resist antidemocratic politicians at the ballot box.

articles.title: Glucosamine, a popular joint supplement, linked to faster Alzheimer’s progression
articles.summary: A large health-record analysis found that glucosamine use was associated with a 25% higher likelihood of mild cognitive impairment progressing to dementia. Lab experiments suggest the popular joint supplement may intensify an abnormal sugar-tagging process in the Alzheimer’s brain, although researchers say clinical trials are needed to determine whether it actually causes harm.

articles.title: Why rheumatoid arthritis pain may persist even when inflammation is under control
articles.summary: Pain and fatigue in rheumatoid arthritis can persist even after inflammation improves, with depression, poor sleep, obesity, smoking, and chronic pain potentially helping sustain symptoms. Researchers say identifying these hidden drivers could prevent unnecessary medication changes and lead to more personalized treatment.

articles.title: REM sleep paradox: Dreaming may drain the brain’s energy even as fuel supply rises
articles.summary: Scientists discovered a surprising energy paradox in the brain during REM sleep, the stage most closely associated with dreaming. Blood supply to the brain begins increasing even before REM starts, but neurons’ immediately available energy, measured as ATP, then drops. The finding suggests that dreaming may require such intense internal processing that neurons consume energy faster than it can be replenished.
